questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A ball is projected off a cliff horizontally with velocity $v$. It lands on the ground a time $t$ later at a distance $d$ from the foot of the cliff as shown. Air resistance is negligible. [Diagram: ball at the top edge of a vertical cliff moving horizontally with velocity $v$; it lands at distance $d$ from the foot of the cliff.] If a heavier ball is projected off the same cliff with the same velocity, which row is correct for the heavier ball? (time to land; distance from foot of cliff) A $t$; $d$ B $t$; less than $d$ C less than $t$; $d$ D less than $t$; less than $d$

stemImage.alt: Question 5: A ball is projected off a cliff horizontally with velocity v. It lands on the ground a time t later at a distance d from the foot of the cliff as shown. Air res

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Standard idea that projectile motion without air resistance is independent of mass.

explanation.body:
As air resistance is negligible, the acceleration ($g$) does not depend on mass, so it does not change.

The time of flight remains the same, and with the same horizontal velocity, the horizontal displacement also remains the same.

perOption.A: Correct. Motion is independent of mass without air resistance.
perOption.B: Horizontal velocity and time are unchanged, so the distance cannot decrease.
perOption.C: A heavier ball does not fall faster; vertical acceleration is $g$ for all masses.
perOption.D: Assumes heavier objects fall faster; both time and distance are unchanged.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A fighter bomber is travelling at $138\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ horizontally at a height of $500\ \mathrm{m}$ above sea level. It is on a bombing run to its target, a naval ship which is moving at $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ away from the bomber. [Diagram: plane at upper right flying left at $138\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $500\ \mathrm{m}$ above sea level; ship at lower left moving left at $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.] Assume negligible air resistance. If the pilot wants to score a direct hit, at which position should he release the bomb? A When the plane is $1010\ \mathrm{m}$ away from the naval ship horizontally. B When the plane is $1270\ \mathrm{m}$ away from the naval ship horizontally. C When the plane is $1390\ \mathrm{m}$ away from the naval ship horizontally. D When the plane is $1510\ \mathrm{m}$ away from the naval ship horizontally.

stemImage.alt: Question 3: A fighter bomber is travelling at 138 m s−1 horizontally at a height of 500 m above sea level. It is on a bombing run to its target, a naval ship which is movin

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combines time of fall with relative horizontal velocity of a moving target.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the target's motion or adding the velocities instead of subtracting

explanation.body:
Vertically the bomb starts with zero velocity: $500 = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.81)t^2$, so $t = 10.1\ \mathrm{s}$ to reach sea level.

In that time the bomb moves $138 \times 10.1 = 1394\ \mathrm{m}$ horizontally, while the ship moves $12 \times 10.1 = 121\ \mathrm{m}$ further away.

So the bomb must be released when the horizontal separation is $1394 - 121 \approx 1270\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses the bomb's horizontal range minus the ship's motion incorrectly (too small a separation).
perOption.B: Correct. Bomb's horizontal range minus the distance the ship moves during the fall.
perOption.C: Ignores the ship's motion: this is just the bomb's horizontal range of about 1390 m.
perOption.D: Adds the ship's displacement instead of subtracting it, though the ship moves in the same direction as the bomb.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A steel ball is falling at constant speed in oil. Which graph shows the variation with time of the gravitational potential energy $E_p$ and the kinetic energy $E_k$ of the ball? [Four energy–time graphs: A $E_k$ horizontal line, $E_p$ decreasing curve getting steeper; B $E_k$ horizontal line, $E_p$ decreasing straight line; C $E_k$ increasing curve from non-zero, $E_p$ decreasing curve getting steeper; D $E_k$ increasing straight line from zero, $E_p$ decreasing straight line.]

stemImage.alt: Question 7: A steel ball is falling at constant speed in oil. Which graph shows the variation with time of the gravitational potential energy Ep and the kinetic energy Ek o

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recognise constant $E_k$ and linear decrease of $E_p$ at terminal velocity.
questions.misconception: Assuming kinetic energy increases as potential energy is lost even at terminal velocity

explanation.body: The ball falls at constant speed, so its kinetic energy remains constant. The resistive force is constant, and the ball falls equal distances in equal times, so its gravitational potential energy decreases linearly.

perOption.A: Shows the gravitational potential energy decreasing at a changing rate.
perOption.C: Shows kinetic energy increasing even though the speed is constant.
perOption.D: Shows kinetic energy increasing even though the speed is constant.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A golfer hits a golf ball so that it leaves the club at an angle of 60° to the horizontal. Assume that air resistance can be ignored. Which graph best represents the variation of kinetic energy and of gravitational potential energy of the ball during the time of flight? [Four energy–time graphs; solid line = kinetic energy, dash-dot = gravitational potential energy; KE starts and ends at the same maximum value, GPE starts and ends at zero. A: KE falls to zero at mid-time, GPE peaks at the full initial value. B: KE and GPE meet at about half the maximum at mid-time. C: KE dips only slightly to about 3/4, GPE peaks at about 1/4. D: KE dips to about 1/4, GPE peaks at about 3/4, curves cross.]

stemImage.alt: Question 8: A golfer hits a golf ball so that it leaves the club at an angle of 60° to the horizontal. Assume that air resistance can be ignored. Which graph best represent

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising the ball still has horizontal KE at the top and estimating its fraction.
questions.misconception: Thinking KE is zero at the top of the trajectory

explanation.body: The total energy is the initial kinetic energy $E=\tfrac12mu^2$. At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, but the constant horizontal velocity is $u\cos60^\circ=u/2$, so the kinetic energy is $\tfrac12m(u/2)^2=E/4$. By energy conservation, the gravitational potential energy there is $3E/4$, so the two curves cross.

perOption.A: Shows zero kinetic energy at the top, as for a vertical launch.
perOption.B: Shows equal energies at the top, as for a $45^\circ$ launch.
perOption.C: Keeps kinetic energy above half the total, as for a launch below $45^\circ$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: An object is dropped from a great height so that air resistance becomes significant. Which graph shows how its acceleration varies with time? [Graphs of acceleration against time: A starts at g and decreases, levelling off at a non-zero value; B starts at 0 and rises to level off at g; C starts at 0, rises to a peak of g, then falls to zero; D starts at g and decreases asymptotically to zero.]

stemImage.alt: Question 2: An object is dropped from a great height so that air resistance becomes significant. Which graph shows how its acceleration varies with time?

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Standard terminal-velocity reasoning applied to an acceleration–time graph.
questions.misconception: Thinking acceleration levels off at a non-zero value, or confusing a–t with v–t

explanation.body: Taking downward as positive, Newton’s second law gives $ma=W-R$, where $R$ is air resistance. At release the speed and air resistance are zero, so $a=g$. As the speed rises, air resistance increases and acceleration falls. When air resistance balances the weight, the acceleration is zero and the object reaches terminal velocity.

perOption.A: A positive final acceleration would mean the object was still speeding up at terminal velocity.
perOption.B: At release, the absence of drag gives an initial acceleration of $g$.
perOption.C: The graph starts at zero, though gravity gives an acceleration of $g$ immediately on release.
perOption.D: Correct. Acceleration falls from $g$ towards zero.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An object is projected horizontally. The object falls a vertical distance y and travels a horizontal distance x before landing on the ground.

A second object is projected horizontally with the same initial velocity and falls a vertical distance 4y before landing on the ground.

Assume that air resistance is negligible.

Which horizontal distance does the second object travel?
questions.stemText: An object is projected horizontally. The object falls a vertical distance y and travels a horizontal distance x before landing on the ground. direction of projection y landing point x A second object is projected horizontally with the same initial velocity and falls a vertical distance 4y before landing on the ground. Assume that air resistance is negligible. Which horizontal distance does the second object travel? A x B 2x C 4x D 16x

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two-step ratio: fall time scales with the square root of height.
questions.misconception: Assuming horizontal distance is proportional to the drop height

explanation.body: The initial vertical speed is zero, so the first fall obeys $y=\tfrac12gt_1^2$ and takes $t_1=\sqrt{2y/g}$. The second fall takes $t_2=\sqrt{2(4y)/g}=2t_1$. The horizontal speed stays constant and is the same for both objects, so the second travels $2x$.

perOption.A: Assumes the same launch speed gives the same time of flight.
perOption.C: Treats the time of flight as directly proportional to the drop height.
perOption.D: Treats horizontal distance as proportional to the square of the drop height.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A hot air balloon is rising vertically at a uniform velocity of $2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. At a height of 10 m above the ground, a ball is thrown out of the hot air balloon horizontally with a velocity of $5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Assume air resistance is negligible.

What is the horizontal distance travelled by the ball before hitting the ground?

A 6.2 m   B 7.1 m   C 7.2 m   D 8.2 m

stemImage.alt: Question 6: 2.0 m s−. At a height of 10 m above 1 A hot air balloon is rising vertically at a uniform velocity of 5.0 m s−. 1 the ground, a ball is thrown out of the hot ai

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must recognise that the ball inherits the upward velocity and then solve a quadratic for the time.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the initial upward velocity inherited from the moving balloon

explanation.body:
Take downwards as positive. When the ball is thrown, it shares the balloon's upward velocity, so $u_y = -2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$:

$s_y = u_y t + \tfrac{1}{2}a_y t^2 \Rightarrow 10 = -2.0t + \tfrac{1}{2}(9.81)t^2$

$t = -1.239\ \mathrm{s}$ (reject) or $t = 1.646\ \mathrm{s}$

Range $= u_x t = 5.0 \times 1.646 = 8.23 \approx 8.2\ \mathrm{m}$

perOption.A: Takes the initial vertical velocity of 2.0 m s$^{-1}$ as downward instead of upward.
perOption.B: Ignores the balloon's upward velocity and treats the ball as starting from vertical rest.
perOption.C: Uses only the time to fall from the highest point and leaves out the time spent rising.
perOption.D: Correct. The ball starts with the balloon's upward velocity of 2.0 m s$^{-1}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A cannon fires a cannonball with an initial speed $v$ at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal. The cannonball reaches a maximum height $H$ and lands at the same horizontal level from which it was fired.

Which expression gives the horizontal range $R$ of the cannonball?

[A dashed projectile trajectory begins and ends on the same horizontal line. The launch velocity $v$ makes angle $\alpha$ with the horizontal, and a vertical arrow marks the apex height $H$.]

A. $R=\frac{2H\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha}$
B. $R=\frac{2H\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha}$
C. $R=\frac{4H\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha}$
D. $R=\frac{4H\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha}$

stemImage.alt: Question 6: A cannon fires a cannonball with an initial speed v at an angle α to the horizontal. The cannonball reaches a maximum height H and lands at the same horizontal

questions.difficultyReason: Requires relating horizontal displacement and vertical rise over the same time and using trajectory symmetry.
questions.misconception: Using the displacement to the apex as the full range

explanation.body: Let $t$ be the time to the highest point. The average vertical velocity gives $H=\tfrac12(v\sin\alpha+0)t$. In the same time the horizontal displacement is $R/2=v\cos\alpha\,t$. Dividing these equations gives $(R/2)/H=2\cos\alpha/\sin\alpha$, so $R=4H\cos\alpha/\sin\alpha$.

perOption.A: Gives the horizontal displacement to the apex only.
perOption.B: Swaps the sine and cosine and gives only half the corresponding range.
perOption.D: Swaps the horizontal and vertical trigonometric factors.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An object is dropped at time $t=0$ from a high building. Air resistance is significant.

Three graphs are plotted against time.

the height of the object above the ground
the speed of the object
the magnitude of the resultant force on the object.

What are the quantities X, Y and Z?

[Graph X starts nearly flat at a positive value, drops and levels off at zero. Graph Y starts nearly flat at a positive value and then falls with a slope that becomes steeper. Graph Z starts at zero, rises and levels off at a positive value. All horizontal axes represent time.]

Options list height above ground, speed and magnitude of resultant force, respectively.
A. X, Y, Z
B. X, Z, Y
C. Y, Z, X
D. Z, Y, X

stemImage.alt: Question 7: An object is dropped at time t = 0 from a high building. Air resistance is significant. Three graphs are plotted against time. the height of the object above th

questions.difficultyReason: Requires matching three graphs by their initial values, slopes and terminal behavior.
questions.misconception: Treating zero net force as zero speed

explanation.body: The object's speed increases at a decreasing rate and eventually levels off at terminal speed, as in Z. X shows the magnitude of the resultant force, which starts at the weight and tends to zero as drag builds. Y shows the height, whose downward slope starts at zero and approaches a constant magnitude as the speed levels off.

perOption.A: Assigns speed to a graph that starts above zero even though the object is dropped from rest.
perOption.B: Swaps height and resultant force, which tends to zero as terminal speed is reached.
perOption.D: Assigns height to an increasing graph although the object is falling.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An object of mass 0.40 kg is projected into the air and follows a curved path above horizontal ground.

The object takes a time of 1.5 s to move along its path. The object lands a horizontal distance of 18 m from its initial position. Air resistance is negligible.

What is the kinetic energy of the object at its maximum height ?
questions.stemText: An object of mass 0.40 kg is projected into the air and follows a curved path above horizontal ground. The object takes a time of 1.5 s to move along its path. The object lands a horizontal distance of 18 m from its initial position. Air resistance is negligible. What is the kinetic energy of the object at its maximum height ? A 0 J B 2.4 J C 11 J D 29 J

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires obtaining the horizontal speed from the range and then calculating the kinetic energy at the apex.
questions.misconception: Assuming all velocity components vanish at the apex

explanation.body: The horizontal velocity is constant, with $u_x=18/1.5=12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. At the highest point the vertical component is zero, so $E_{\mathrm k}=\tfrac12 m u_x^2=\tfrac12(0.40)(12)^2=28.8\ \mathrm{J}$, or $29\ \mathrm{J}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Treats zero vertical velocity at the apex as zero total velocity.
perOption.B: Uses the horizontal speed without squaring it in the kinetic energy formula.
perOption.C: Uses the launch vertical speed of about $7.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in place of the horizontal speed at the apex.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The diagram shows the trajectory of a projectile and the velocity $v$ of the projectile at point P in its trajectory. P is located before the projectile reaches the peak altitude. Air resistance acts on the projectile. The acceleration of the projectile at P is $a$.

[The dashed trajectory rises from left to right above a horizontal ground line. At P, the tangent velocity arrow $v$ points up and to the right.]

What are the magnitudes of the horizontal component and the vertical component of the acceleration of the projectile at P?

Horizontal component of $a$ | Vertical component of $a$
A Zero | Greater than $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
B Non-zero | Greater than $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
C Zero | $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
D Non-zero | $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 10: The diagram shows the trajectory of a projectile and the velocity v of the projectile at point P in its trajectory. P is located before the projectile reaches t

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires resolving the drag force and combining its vertical component with weight.
questions.misconception: Applying the no-drag acceleration components when drag is present

explanation.body: At P, the drag force acts opposite to the upward and forward velocity, so it has a horizontal component and a downward component. The horizontal acceleration is therefore non-zero. The downward component of drag adds to the weight, making the vertical acceleration greater than $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ in magnitude.

perOption.A: Ignores the horizontal component of drag.
perOption.C: Uses the acceleration components for a projectile with negligible air resistance.
perOption.D: Includes the horizontal drag but omits the downward component of drag.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An eagle is flying horizontally at 6.00 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ with a fish in its claws. It accidentally drops the fish.

How much time passes before the fish’s speed doubles? Neglect air resistance.
questions.stemText: An eagle is flying horizontally at 6.00 m s−1 with a fish in its claws. It accidentally drops the fish. How much time passes before the fish’s speed doubles? Neglect air resistance. A 0.500 s B 1.06 s C 2.12 s D 4.00 s
questions.difficultyReason: The final speed must be resolved into components before using the vertical motion equation.
questions.misconception: Treating gravity as an acceleration along the velocity

explanation.body: The final speed is $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, with horizontal component $v_x=6.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. From $v_x^2+v_y^2=12^2$, we get $36+v_y^2=144$, giving a downward component of $10.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Using $v_y=u_y+at$ downwards gives $10.4=0+9.81t$, so $t=1.06\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Treats the increase in total speed as the vertical velocity gained, underestimating the time.
perOption.C: Doubles the time obtained from the vertical velocity gain.
perOption.D: Overestimates the time required for gravity to build the vertical component to $10.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two coins are projected from a horizontal table at the same initial speed $u$.
Coin X is projected horizontally.
Coin Y is projected upwards at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal.

Both coins hit the horizontal ground without bouncing.
Assume the air resistance on each coin is negligible.
Which statement about the motion of the coins is correct?

A Both coins hit the ground with the same speed.
B Both coins travel the same vertical distance.
C Coin Y hits the ground before coin X.
D Coin Y has a smaller vertical acceleration.

stemImage.alt: Question 7: Two coins are projected from a horizontal table at the same initial speed u. Coin X is projected horizontally. Coin Y is projected upwards at an angle of 30 to

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires relating impact speed to energy while distinguishing vertical distance from displacement.
questions.misconception: Assuming launch direction changes impact speed.

explanation.body: Both coins start with the same speed and fall through the same net height. By conservation of energy, they gain the same kinetic energy per unit mass and therefore hit the ground with the same speed.

perOption.B: Y rises before falling, so it travels a greater vertical distance.
perOption.C: Y takes longer to reach the ground because it initially moves upwards.
perOption.D: With negligible air resistance, both coins have the same downward acceleration.
